questions.text: What are the 'requirements' numbered 2 to 8 that the document cites? Where are they defined, and what is requirement 1?
questions.about: Rules not shown on the arrows (requirement 3, 2, 4...)

questions.text: The login gate records the attempt before the password is checked, and the failure script checks again after a wrong password. Does a correct-password login also leave its attempt in the lf set until it is deleted? And how can the fifth failing request still get 401 if the gate already counts more than 5 as locked?

The gate step says the lock is set when the set holds more than 5 entries, and the failure script sets it at 5 or more. Which is the real threshold, and how many wrong passwords does it take before the 429 starts?
questions.about: Login gate (requirement 3) and FAIL(email) in the sequence diagram

questions.text: What does the app do when the old-session DEL succeeds or fails, relative to the new session already created? The doc says to create new first, then delete old. What happens if the new session creation succeeds but the user never receives the 302?

The session record has abs_expires_at and the app compares it to the Redis clock. Is that comparison done in the Lua script or in app code? And what does the app send back to the browser when a deleted user is detected after CHECK succeeds?

Is the Lua script an actual single call per step (GATE, CHECK, create session)? How does the app instance load and call these scripts, and what is DEL lf and the plain DEL of the session: scripts or direct commands?
questions.about: GATE(email), CHECK(sha256 sid), create new sess record

questions.text: What does the cookie being a browser-session cookie mean for a user who closes the browser and reopens it within 30 minutes? Is the server session still alive, and can they be signed back in?
Does the login page (GET /login) and other unprotected pages call CHECK? The diagram says 'any page except /login'; what does a logged-in user visiting /login see?
An email is 'capped at 254 characters' before hashing. Does that mean a longer email is cut to 254 characters, or is it refused? And is the Postgres lookup done with the cut or the original email?
questions.about: State in Redis (notes: emails trimmed, lowercased, capped at 254 characters)

questions.text: What does the app do when POST /login arrives with the email or password field missing or empty? Does it go through the gate and count as an attempt, and what response comes back?
questions.about: Login (POST /login), the first steps before the GATE script

questions.text: Each login attempt is one entry in the lf sorted set, with the time in ms as the score. What is the entry's member value? Two attempts in the same millisecond must both count, so how are they kept apart?
questions.about: State in Redis: lf:{sha256(email)} sorted set, GATE step 4

teachbacks.text:
Walkthrough: a user logs in, views the dashboard, then logs out.

Setup: A server-rendered app runs as two identical instances behind a load balancer with no sticky sessions. Postgres holds the `users` table (id, lowercase unique email, bcrypt password_hash). One shared Redis holds sessions and login-attempt counters, so either instance can serve any request.

Part A. Login (POST /login)

1. Start. The browser submits the login form as `POST /login` with email and password. It may also send an old `__Host-sid` cookie if it already has one. Either instance can receive it. The app has no state of its own here.

2. Normalize the email. The app trims and lowercases the email and caps it at 254 characters. The key names in Redis are built from the SHA-256 of this email. Known and unknown emails therefore get the same kind of keys.

3. Rate-limit gate. The app runs the GATE Lua script in Redis, before looking at the password. The script runs atomically and uses the Redis clock.
   - If `lock:{sha256(email)}` exists, it returns LOCKED.
   - Otherwise it drops entries older than 10 minutes from the sorted set `lf:{sha256(email)}`.
   - If 5 or more entries remain, it sets the lock with `SET NX EX 900` and returns LOCKED.
   - Otherwise it adds this attempt to the set, refreshes the set's 10-minute TTL and returns OK.
   - The attempt is recorded before anyone knows whether the password is right.

4. If LOCKED. The app replies 429 with the login page and `Retry-After: 900`. The password is not checked. The response is the same for any email. This is the end of the request.

5. If OK. The app queries Postgres with `SELECT id, password_hash FROM users WHERE email = ?`. Postgres returns a row or no row. The app then runs a bcrypt compare. If there was no row, it compares against a fixed dummy hash so the timing looks the same.

6. If the email is unknown or the password is wrong. The app returns 401 with the login page showing "Invalid email or password". The text is identical for both cases and no cookie is set. Nothing more is written to Redis, because the gate already counted the attempt. Five wrong attempts are allowed. The 6th finds 5 entries, starts the 15-minute lock and gets 429.

7. If the password is correct, the app does these steps in order:
   a. It runs `DEL lf:{email}`. This clears all earlier failures and this attempt. If it fails, the reply is 503 and no session is created.
   b. It runs the CREATE script with a new random ID (32 bytes from a CSPRNG, base64url). The script stores a hash at `sess:{sha256(id)}` with `user_id`, `created_at` and `abs_expires_at` (now + 12 h). It sets the TTL to 30 minutes.
   c. If the request carried an old cookie, the app runs `DEL` on the old session. If that delete fails, the app tries to delete the new session and returns 503. This prevents session fixation.
   d. The app replies `302 /dashboard` with `Set-Cookie: __Host-sid=<new id>; Path=/; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax`. The cookie has no Domain, Max-Age or Expires.

8. If the 302 never reaches the browser. The new ID is unknown to anyone and expires by its idle TTL. The old session is already gone, so the user sees the login page and logs in again.

Part B. Protected request (for example GET /dashboard)

9. Start. The browser sends `GET /dashboard` with the cookie. Every route except GET /login, POST /login and POST /logout does the following.

10. Session check. The app runs the CHECK script with the SHA-256 of the cookie ID. It runs atomically on the Redis clock.
    - If the key is missing, it returns MISSING.
    - If `now >= abs_expires_at`, it deletes the session and returns MISSING.
    - Otherwise it sets the TTL to `min(1800, abs_expires_at - now)` and returns the `user_id`. This restarts the 30-minute idle clock on every request but never runs past the 12-hour deadline.

11. If MISSING (no cookie, unknown ID or expired). The app replies `302 /login` with a `Set-Cookie` that clears the cookie.

12. If valid. The app loads the user row from Postgres to render the page.
    - If the row exists, the reply is 200 with the page.
    - If the row was deleted, the app treats the request as unauthenticated. It runs `DEL` on the session (best effort), clears the cookie and replies `302 /login`.

13. If Redis errors during CHECK. The reply is 503, and the cookie is not cleared and there is no redirect. The reason given is that the session may still be valid.

Part C. Logout (POST /logout)

14. Start. The browser sends `POST /logout`, with or without a cookie. This route never calls CHECK.

15. If a cookie was sent, the app runs `DEL sess:{sha256(id)}`. Deleting a key that is already gone is not an error.

16. If Redis errors on the delete. The reply is 503 saying logout could not be completed. The cookie is kept and the user can retry.

17. Otherwise. The reply is `302 /login` with a `Set-Cookie` that clears `__Host-sid` (same name, path and flags, `Max-Age=0`). This happens whether or not a session existed.

Other behaviours stated in the document:
- Redis and Postgres failures during login give 503 with the page "Sign-in is temporarily unavailable. Please try again in a few minutes." and no cookie. All of these fail closed.
- A Postgres failure during login is not counted as a bad credential and does not return 401. The gate already counted the attempt.
- Each app instance loads the three Lua scripts at startup with `SCRIPT LOAD` and runs them with `EVALSHA`. On `NOSCRIPT` it reloads and retries once.
- Abandoned sessions disappear by Redis TTL. There is no sweeper job.
- Redis runs with AOF `appendfsync everysec` and `maxmemory-policy noeviction`.
- The `SameSite=Lax` cookie is what the document relies on for CSRF protection of POSTs.
- Closing the browser normally deletes the cookie, since it is a browser-session cookie.
- A signed-in user who opens /login just sees the login page.
gaps: The document does not say what the 401 and 429 login pages look like beyond the message text. It does not say whether the submitted email is kept in the form.
It does not say how the app tells the cookie is absent or malformed, or what it does with an overlong or garbage cookie value, beyond 'missing or unknown'.
It does not say what the dashboard or other protected pages contain, or what routes exist besides /login, /logout and /dashboard.
It does not say how the load balancer picks an instance, or how the app instances are configured to find Redis and Postgres.
It does not say what happens if CREATE succeeds but the later old-session DEL fails and the best-effort cleanup of the new session also fails. The new session would then live until its TTL expires.
It does not say what happens if the Redis NOSCRIPT retry also fails.
It does not say how a Redis failure during the 429 lock write is reported, or what Retry-After is given for a lock that is already partly elapsed. It always says 900.
The document does not say what the 503 pages show for protected requests beyond 'temporary error page', and it does not say whether the login 503 resets the form.
It does not say how the bcrypt cost, the dummy hash value or the database connection handling are chosen.
It does not say how the app obtains the random bytes or how the SHA-256 and base64url steps are implemented (library, language), or what the app's language or framework is.
It does not say how the 12-hour absolute limit is surfaced to the user, such as a message on the login page after expiry.
It does not say whether the session user_id is re-checked against anything other than row existence, for example if the password changes.
teachbacks.notes: Double failure in login step 3 (old-session DEL fails and best-effort delete of the new session also fails) was not spelled out: the document did not say the orphaned new session is harmless because nobody learns its ID.; A failed NOSCRIPT retry (or script load failure) was not covered: it was not stated to count as a Redis error that fails closed.; Redis failure while GATE writes the lock was not stated to be a plain GATE failure (503), and Retry-After was always 900 even for a partly elapsed lock; it should be the lock's remaining time.; Handling of absent, malformed or overlong cookie values was not defined; now stated as treated like no cookie, without calling Redis.; Whether the login pages keep the submitted email, what the 503 pages show, and which things (framework, bcrypt cost, page contents, password-change invalidation, expiry messages) are deliberately out of scope were not stated.

teachbacks.text:
Walkthrough: a user logs in, views the dashboard, then logs out (all from the document only).

1. Browser sends POST /login with email, password, and possibly an old `__Host-sid` cookie. Either app instance can take it (load balancer, no sticky sessions). The app trims and lowercases the email (capped at 254 chars). Nothing is stored yet; state lives in Redis (sessions, failure counts, locks) and Postgres (users).

2. The app runs the GATE Lua script in Redis, keyed by sha256(email). Redis is shared by both instances. GATE runs before any password check. It does this atomically:
 a. If `lock:{sha256(email)}` exists, return LOCKED with remaining seconds.
 b. Drop entries older than 10 min from the sorted set `lf:{sha256(email)}`.
 c. If the set already has 5 or more entries, set the lock (SET NX EX 900) and return LOCKED with 900 s (or the remaining time if another instance set it first).
 d. Otherwise add this attempt (score = Redis time in ms), refresh the set's 10-minute TTL, and return OK.
 The attempt is counted whether or not the password turns out right. The app loads the script at startup with SCRIPT LOAD and runs it with EVALSHA. On NOSCRIPT it reloads and retries once.

3. Failure at the gate. If Redis errors (including a failed lock write), the app returns 503 with the "Sign-in is temporarily unavailable" login page, email kept, no cookie, password not checked. If GATE returned LOCKED, the app returns 429 with the login form plus a message, with `Retry-After` set to the remaining seconds, and the password is not checked. So 5 wrong passwords get 401 and the 6th attempt gets 429.

4. If GATE returned OK, the app queries Postgres: SELECT id, password_hash FROM users WHERE email = ?. It then does a bcrypt compare. If there is no row it compares against a fixed dummy bcrypt hash so timing is the same. If Postgres fails, the app returns the same 503 page. That is not a 401, but the attempt still counts.

5. Wrong password or unknown email. The app returns 401 with the login form, the message "Invalid email or password", the email kept, an empty password field, and no cookie. The two cases are identical. Nothing more is recorded because the gate already counted the attempt.

6. Correct password. The app does the following in order:
 a. `DEL lf:{email}`, which clears all earlier failures including this attempt. If it fails, 503 and no session is created.
 b. Run the CREATE script with a fresh 32-byte CSPRNG ID (base64url, 43 chars). It writes the hash `sess:{sha256(id)}` with user_id, created_at=now and abs_expires_at=now+12h. It sets a 30-minute TTL.
 c. If the request carried an old cookie, `DEL` the old session. If that fails, it tries to delete the new session, best effort, and returns 503.
 d. Reply 302 /dashboard with `Set-Cookie: __Host-sid=<newid>; Path=/; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax`, no Domain, no Max-Age/Expires.
 Any Redis error here gives 503 with no cookie, and the user can retry. If the 302 is lost in the network, the new session is never used and expires after 30 minutes idle.

7. Browser follows to GET /dashboard with the cookie. This is a protected request, and every route except GET /login, POST /login and POST /logout is protected. If the cookie value is not exactly 43 base64url characters, the app makes no Redis call and treats it as missing.

8. The app runs the CHECK script with sha256(id). It runs atomically on the Redis clock:
 a. If the key is absent, return MISSING.
 b. If now >= abs_expires_at, delete the session and return MISSING.
 c. Otherwise set the TTL to min(1800, abs_expires_at - now) and return user_id. This restarts the idle clock on every request.

9. Outcomes of CHECK:
 - MISSING (no cookie, malformed, unknown, idle-expired or past 12 h): reply Set-Cookie clearing `__Host-sid` (same name, path and flags, Max-Age=0) and 302 /login, with no reason given.
 - Redis error: 503 "temporarily unavailable" page. The cookie is kept and there is no redirect, because the session may still be valid.
 - Valid: the app loads the user row from Postgres. If the row exists, it returns 200 with the page. If the row was deleted, it does a best-effort DEL of the session, clears the cookie and replies 302 /login.

10. Logout. The browser sends POST /logout. If a valid-looking cookie came, the app runs `DEL sess:{sha256(id)}`. Deleting a missing key is not an error. On success, or with no session, the reply is the clearing Set-Cookie plus 302 /login. If Redis errors, it returns a 503 "could not log out" page, the cookie is kept, and the user can retry. SameSite=Lax is stated to cover CSRF for this scope.

11. Session lifetime. A session ends after 30 minutes with no requests, or 12 hours after login, whichever comes first. Redis TTL removes abandoned records (no sweeper). Because the cookie has no expiry, it is usually dropped when the browser closes, though the server record may linger up to 30 minutes.
gaps: The document says the Redis clock is used for times and that GATE and CHECK use TIME, but does not say how the app learns the remaining lock seconds when LOCKED (it only says the script returns them).

Does not say how a successful login treats an existing lock created between GATE and DEL (it says login cannot succeed while locked, but nothing on what happens to lf entries after a concurrent lock).

Does not say how the CREATE script returns the new ID or whether the app generates the ID before calling CREATE (the text says the app 'runs CREATE with a fresh ID', implying the app generates it, but the diagram says the script is given it; where randomness is generated is not stated explicitly).
Does not specify the exact HTTP content of the 429 and 503 pages beyond 'login page with message'; the exact 429 message text is not given.

Does not say what a signed-in user's 'old sid' cookie value must look like to count as 'carried a cookie' at login (malformed cookie treated as no cookie is stated generally, but the login step 3 condition is not explicit).

Does not describe how the app validates the session ID format or hashes it in detail beyond 'exactly 43 base64url characters' and SHA-256 (hex vs raw encoding of the hash in key names is not specified).
Does not state what happens if Postgres fails on a protected request when loading the user row (only Redis failure and a missing row are covered).
Does not state how the load balancer, TLS termination or the Secure/__Host- cookie requirement of HTTPS is arranged; the load balancing method is left to the implementer.
Does not say what the login page does for a GET /login beyond rendering the form, or what CSRF handling exists for POST /login (only the SameSite=Lax argument for cookie-bearing posts).
The 'Retry-After' for a lock set by another instance is described as 'remaining time', but the unit conversion and rounding are not specified.
teachbacks.notes: The document never said how the app gets the lock's remaining seconds from GATE (return shape) or the unit/rounding for Retry-After.; It did not say what happens when another instance sets a lock between this request's GATE and its DEL lf after a correct password.; It was unclear who generates the session ID (app vs CREATE script) and what CREATE takes and returns; the text and diagram disagreed in wording.; The 429 message text was not given.; The login-time condition for 'carried a cookie' was not explicit (should use the same 43-character validity rule).; The SHA-256 encoding used in key names (hex vs raw) was not specified.; Postgres failure when loading the user row on a protected request was not covered.; HTTPS/TLS assumption needed by Secure and the __Host- prefix was not stated.; GET /login behaviour and CSRF handling on POST /login were not stated.

teachbacks.text:
1. Setup. Two identical app instances sit behind a load balancer with no sticky sessions. They share one Redis (sessions, failure counts, locks) and one Postgres (the `users` table: id, lowercase unique email, bcrypt password_hash). Each instance loads three Lua scripts (GATE, CREATE, CHECK) with SCRIPT LOAD at startup and runs them with EVALSHA. On NOSCRIPT it reloads and retries once. If that fails, it counts as an ordinary Redis error. Browsers are assumed to use HTTPS.

2. Login starts. The browser sends `POST /login` with email and password. It may also send an old `__Host-sid` cookie. The app reads the form fields, and a missing field becomes an empty string. It trims and lowercases the email. If the email is over 254 characters, it cuts it to 254 and uses the cut string only as the gate key. It hashes the key with SHA-256 to get the "email hash". It also makes a fresh 16-byte random attempt nonce. The cookie only counts if it is exactly 43 base64url characters. Otherwise it is treated as absent.

3. The gate. The app calls the GATE script with the email hash and the nonce. GATE runs atomically in Redis and uses the Redis clock. It checks the following in order.
   - If `lock:{hash}` exists, it returns LOCKED with the remaining seconds, rounded up, minimum 1.
   - Otherwise it drops entries older than 10 minutes from the sorted set `lf:{hash}`.
   - If the set already has 5 or more entries, it sets the lock with `SET NX EX 900` and returns LOCKED. The remaining time is 900 seconds, or less if another instance set the lock first.
   - Otherwise it adds this attempt (member = nonce, score = time in ms), refreshes the set's 10-minute TTL, and returns OK.
   
   So the first 5 attempts in a window pass, and the 6th gets 429.

4. Gate outcomes.
   - If GATE hits a Redis error, the app returns 503 with the login form, the email kept, and no cookie. The password is not checked.
   - If GATE returns LOCKED, the app returns 429 with the login form, the message "Too many sign-in attempts. Please try again later." and `Retry-After` set to the remaining seconds. The password is not checked.
   - If GATE returns OK, the app continues.

5. User lookup and password check. If the email is non-empty and 254 characters or fewer, the app queries Postgres with `SELECT id, password_hash FROM users WHERE email = ?`. Otherwise it skips the query. It then runs a bcrypt comparison. If there is no row, it compares against a fixed dummy hash, so timing looks the same. A Postgres failure here gives the same 503 as a Redis login failure. It is not a 401, but the attempt was already counted.

6. Failure path. For an unknown email or a wrong password, the app returns 401 with the login form, the message "Invalid email or password", the email kept and the password empty. It sets no cookie, and both cases look identical. Nothing more is recorded, because the gate already counted the attempt.

7. Success path. This runs only after the gate passed and the bcrypt check succeeded, in this order.
   1. `DEL lf:{hash}` clears all earlier failures, including this attempt. If it fails, the app returns 503 and creates no session. The lock key is not touched.
   2. The app generates a new 32-byte CSPRNG ID, base64url encoded to 43 characters.
   3. It calls CREATE with sha256(ID) and user_id. CREATE writes the hash `sess:{sha256(id)}` with user_id, created_at and abs_expires_at (now + 12 h), and sets a 30-minute TTL.
   4. If the request carried a valid-looking old cookie, the app runs `DEL` on the old session. If that fails, it tries to delete the new session (best effort) and returns 503.
   5. It replies `302 /dashboard` with `Set-Cookie: __Host-sid=<new id>; Path=/; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax`. There is no Domain, Max-Age or Expires.
   
   Any Redis error in steps 1 to 4 gives a 503 with the login form and no cookie, and the user can retry. If the 302 never reaches the browser, the new session expires by its idle TTL, and the user just logs in again.

8. Protected request. The browser sends `GET /dashboard` (or any page except GET/POST /login and POST /logout) with the cookie. If the cookie is missing or malformed, no Redis call is made. The app clears the cookie (`Max-Age=0`) and replies `302 /login`. Otherwise it calls CHECK with sha256(id). CHECK runs atomically on the Redis clock.
   - If the key is missing, it returns MISSING.
   - If now >= abs_expires_at, it deletes the session and returns MISSING.
   - Otherwise it resets the TTL to min(1800, abs_expires_at - now) and returns user_id.
   
   Because every protected request goes through CHECK, every request restarts the 30-minute idle clock. The 12-hour cap is never exceeded.

9. After CHECK. On MISSING (no cookie, unknown, expired), the app replies with a Set-Cookie that clears the cookie, then `302 /login`, with no reason given. On a user_id, the app loads the user row from Postgres.
   - If the row exists, the app returns the 200 page.
   - If the row is gone, the app does a best-effort `DEL` of the session, clears the cookie, and replies `302 /login`.
   - If Postgres or Redis fails at this point, the app returns a 503 "temporarily unavailable" page and keeps the cookie, because the session may still be valid.

10. Logout. The browser sends `POST /logout`. If a valid-looking cookie is present, the app runs `DEL sess:{sha256(id)}`. Deleting a missing key is not an error. If Redis fails, the app returns a 503 saying logout could not be completed and keeps the cookie, so the user can retry. Otherwise the app always replies with a Set-Cookie that clears the cookie and `302 /login`, whether or not a session existed. SameSite=Lax is the CSRF defence for this scope.

11. Cleanup and durability. There is no sweeper job. Redis TTLs remove abandoned sessions and old failure sets. The lock expires after 15 minutes and is never extended. Redis runs with AOF `appendfsync everysec` and `maxmemory-policy noeviction`. When Redis is full it returns errors, and the app fails closed. Closing the browser usually drops the session cookie. The server session lingers up to 30 minutes idle but is unreachable. All 503s are logged with the error but without the email or session ID.
gaps: The document does not say what happens to a session or lock key if a Lua script is killed or times out mid-run. It only says any Redis error is handled as a failure.

The document does not name any HTTP status code or page for malformed requests beyond saying there is no separate bad-request response. Behaviour for a wrong HTTP method, or for oversized bodies, is left to the implementer's body size limit.
The document does not say how the CHECK or GATE scripts are given the key names. It only says what the app passes in, such as the hash, and the key prefixes are given only in the State table.
The document does not say what the CREATE script returns on error, or what happens if CREATE is called with an ID that already exists. It says only that the ID is random and never reused.
The document does not say how the app converts bcrypt results or what cost value is used. It says only to use the cost of the existing hashes.
The document does not say what the `/dashboard` page contains or what user data it loads beyond 'the user row'. It also does not say what other protected routes exist.
The document does not describe the load balancer's behaviour beyond 'no sticky sessions', and it does not describe how TLS and HTTPS are provided. It explicitly leaves this out.
The document does not say how the app decides which instance's clock matters for the lock's remaining seconds when another instance set it. It says only that Redis time is used.
The document does not say what the 12-hour expiry looks like to the user. It says only that the user is redirected to login with no message.
The document does not say how Redis-backed login behaves when GATE returns an unexpected value other than OK or LOCKED.
teachbacks.notes: Script failure modes unclear: a Lua script killed or timed out mid-run, and an unexpected GATE/CHECK/CREATE return value, were not covered.; CREATE's error result and what happens if the session ID already exists were not stated.; How the scripts receive key names (app passes hashes; the script builds the key with the fixed prefix) was not stated.; Which clock decides the lock's remaining seconds was not explicit (single Redis clock, PTTL).; What the user sees on a 12-hour expiry was only in the implementer section, not with the protected-request rules.; Behaviour for wrong HTTP methods, unknown routes and oversized bodies was not stated; also what counts as a protected route and what /dashboard contains.; Bcrypt cost/dummy hash and TLS/load balancer were reported as unexplained; they are deliberately left to the implementer, but the document should say so at the point of use.
